name: Faience
lede: Faience is the glazed blue-green ceramic of ancient Egypt, a material that may have helped start glassmaking; the same word later named tin-glazed European earthenware, and a mid blue in a 1930 color dictionary.

sections.title: Egyptian faience
sections.body:
Ball describes Egyptian faience as a blue glassy coating made from about 4500 BC in the Middle East, first on soapstone ornaments meant to imitate the costly blue mineral [[lapis-lazuli]] [1]. Makers powdered the surface of the stone and heated it with copper minerals such as azurite or malachite [1]. Despite the name, Ball notes, it was made in Mesopotamia long before Egypt turned it into an industry [1]. By 3000 BC it was being made along the lower Nile, and about 1,500 years later trade had spread it across Europe [1].

In faience proper the copper mineral is mixed into the body of the object, while in a true glaze it is applied to the surface of a finished piece [1]. Later Egyptian makers used glass made from sand and soda ash as the vehicle for the faience technique, and some of the earliest clay glazes were beads fired with soda and copper minerals [1]. Ball thinks it highly likely that the kiln technology of blue-glazed objects led to the smelting of copper from its ore, and it may have helped to stimulate glass and the Egyptian blue pigment [1].

Pastoureau adds the meaning side. The Egyptians made blue and blue-green faience into funerary pieces, such as statuettes, figurines and beads, and the color itself was thought to carry magical or protective force [2]. Blue and green were so close in Egyptian culture that it is hard to tell them apart on some of the statuettes [2]. Not all faience was blue, either: Birren cites Budge on red faience rings and amulets found in Egyptian tombs, though nobody knows how they were used [3].

sections.title: One word, two materials
sections.body:
The word later moved on. The Pigment Compendium uses faience for tin-enamelled earthenware, a different material from the Egyptian one, and traces the glaze technique to Italy via Spain by the fourteenth century, spreading to northern Europe in wares such as [[delft-blue]] [4]. It links the term to an Arabic phrase for Egyptian alum or soda, by way of the glaze name *marzachotto*, though the derivation is hedged as probable [4].

The books therefore use one word for two different things, and a reader should check which one is meant before assuming blue-green.

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body:
The color here, a mid blue with a touch of green, comes from the Maerz and Paul dictionary of 1930, which records the name in 1923 on plate 35 [5]. It is closest to [[cerulean]] among our names [5]. A screen swatch is only an approximation, and Egyptian faience itself ranges from blue to green [2][5].

Where to look: a museum case of Egyptian beads or a *shabti* figure shows the original material, and the variation from blue to green in a single piece is part of its character [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our painting archive the color appears in 78 of 23,781 paintings, 0.33 per cent, and is rarer than 55 per cent of the named colors [6]. It is mostly an accent, which is how it plays in 48 per cent of the 33 paintings in the within-painting count [6]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 0.4 per cent of the 1,674 paintings from then, 2.7 times the museums' baseline [6]. The earliest match is a 1482 work by Piero di Cosimo, a look-alike hue in an aged photograph and not evidence of the material [6].

What was blue faience first made to imitate?

openers: Egyptian faience was invented to imitate lapis lazuli, and it was made in Mesopotamia before Egypt.
The same word names two different materials: the Egyptian glazed paste and the tin-glazed European earthenware.
